lines.text: אדה 13 אדן
* אָדָה obsol. root, prob. i. q. אָזָה and
עָדָה to pass.—Hence אֲדִין.
אִדּוֹ pr. n. Iddo, Ezra 8, 17. R. אָדַר.
אֱדוֹם see אֱדֹם.
אָדוֹן m. (r. אָדַן q. v.) with suff. and in
plur. defect. אֲדֹנֵי, אֲדֹנִים; with pref.
בַּאדֹנִי, וַאדֹנִי, לַאדֹנִי; master, lord, do-
minus. Spoken a) Of an owner, pos-
sessor, 1 K. 16, 21 owner of mount Shom-
ron, i. e. Samaria. Hence of the owner
and master of slaves, Gen. 24, 14. 27. 39,
2. 7; of kings as the lords of their sub-
jects, Is. 26, 13; of a husband as lord of
the wife, Gen. 18, 12, comp. בַּעַל and Gr.
κύριος γυναικός, Germ. Eheherr. Also
of God as the owner and governor of
the world, Josh. 3, 13 אֲדוֹן כָּל־הָאָרֶץ,
Lord of the whole earth; hence called
κατ᾽ ἐξοχήν הָאָדוֹן Ex. 23, 17, and with-
out art. אָדוֹן Ps. 114, 7; comp. אֲדֹנָי
in next art. b) Of a ruler, governor,
Gen. 45, 8. So אֲדֹנִי my lord! an honor-
ary title of address to nobles and others
to whom honour and reverence are due;
e. g. to a father Gen. 31, 35, a brother
Num. 12, 11, to a royal consort 1 K. 1,
17. 18; espec. to kings and princes, as
respectfully addressing a person, the
Hebrews, instead of the second personal
pron. thou, were accustomed to say my
lord, and instead of the first person, thy
servant, thy handmaid, Gen. 33, 8. 13, 14.
15. 44, 7. 9. 19 אֲדֹנִי שָׁאַל אֶת־עֲבָדָיו my
lord asked his servants, i. e. thou didst
ask us. In a style of still stronger adu-
lation, this mode of speaking is also used
in the case of an absent person, as Gen.
Plur. אֲדֹנִים masters, lords, Is. 26, 13
with a verb plural; and so c. suff. ־ַי, אֲדֹנַי
i. e. my lords Gen. 19, 2. 18. Elsewhere
the plural forms אֲדֹנִים, אֲדֹנֵי, c. suff.
־ֶיךָ, ־ָיו, ־ֵיכֶם, etc. are always plur.
excellentiæ, and of the same signif. as
the sing. Gen. 39, 2 sq. Hence joined
with an adj. in the sing. number, as Is.
19, 4 אֲדֹנִים קָשֶׁה a hard master, cruel
lord. Gen. 42, 30. 33 אֲדֹנֵי הָאָרֶץ lord
of the land. אֲדֹנֶיךָ thy master 2 K. 2, 3.
5. 16. Ps. 45, 12; אֲדֹנָיו his master Gen.
17 אֲדֹנֵי הָאֲדֹנִים Lord of lords, i. e. Je-
hovah. Ps. 136, 3. Spoken of idols,
Zeph. 1, 9; comp. בַּעַל.
Note. This word is wanting in all
the kindred dialects, except the Pheni-
cian, where it is applied to princes,
kings, and gods, see Monumenta Phœnic.
p. 346 (comp. Ἄδων, Ἄδωνις, Hesych.
κύριος); and perhaps the Chaldean,
where a vestige of it seems to be pre-
served in the pr. n. בִּלְאֲדָן.
אֲדֹנָי Lord, the Lord, spoken every
where κατ᾽ ἐξοχήν of God, chiefly (in the
Pentat. always) where God is submis-
sively and reverently addressed; as in
the formulas בִּי אֲדֹנָי Ex. 4, 10. 13. Josh.
7, 8; אָנָּא אֲדֹנָי Neh. 1, 11, comp. Gen. 15,
2. 18, 30–32. Ex. 34, 9. etc. Then also
where God is spoken of, 1 K. 13, 10. 22,
quently other divine names are added;
as אֲדֹנָי יְהוִֹה (which the Masorites write
אֲדֹנָי יֱהוִֹה) Is. 40, 10. Jer. 2, 22; אֲדֹנָי
הָאֱלֹהִים Dan. 9, 13.—As to the ending ־ָי
grammarians differ in opinion. Many
regard it as a plural form put for the
sing. as spoken of the divine majesty
(pluralis excellentiæ), i. q. אֲדֹנִים, the
Kamets being put for Pattah to distin-
guish it from אֲדֹנַי my lords; see Gram.
§ 86. 1. c. § 106. 2. b. Others consider
־ָי i. q. ־ַי, and make it strictly a suffix
plural; so that אֲדֹנָי is pr. my lords,
then as plur. excell. my Lord, and at
last, the force of the suffix being by de-
grees neglected, Lord, the Lord, ὁ Κύ
ριος. Comp. Syr. ܡܳܪܝ and Fr. Mon-
sieur. This latter view seems prefer-
able, for the following reasons: a) The
words of Ps. 35, 23 אֱלֹהַי וַאדֹנָי. 16, 2.
b) The ancient usage of the Pentat.
where it is for the Voc. my Lord! c) A
similar usage in possessive pronouns,
afterwards neglected, in the Phenician
names of gods, as אֲדֹנִי Ἄδωνις, בעלתי
Βαάλτις, for which see Monum. Phœnic.
never has the article, and so nouns with
a suffix.—To all this it might be an-
swered: α) That אֲדֹנָי is plural. But
in one place only is it coupled with a
plural, Gen. 19, 2; in the two remaining
passages it is singular, my Lord! Gen.
18, 3. 19, 18. β) That God twice calls
himself אֲדֹנָי, Is. 8, 7. Job 28, 28. But

line_status.note: The left-hand letter of the right-column word is a narrow vertical stroke descending below the baseline of the dalet (final nun ן), not the wide rounded-shoulder resh ר of this font; so the header reads אדן, as in Reading B. No vowel points are printed in the header.

The middle letter of the second Hebrew word has a wide flat head overhanging the stem on both sides — a zayin (ז), not a vav; contrast the narrow hooked ו in the running head אוה above. Reading B matches the print.
The last word on the printed line ends in a final nun with hireq under the dalet (אֲדִין), not the Iddo form אִדּוֹ, which belongs to the start of line 3.
Final root letter is ר (no left leg, unlike the ה in אָדָה above) with patach under the dalet: אָדַר, as in B; A's אָדָה is wrong.
The vowel under the aleph of the second (defective) word is a hataf segol (two vertical dots plus segol cluster), matching the first word, not a qamets; both words point to the entry אֱדֹם Edom.

Under the nun of the first Hebrew word (אֲדֹנֵי) the print has two dots side by side — tsere, the construct plural — not a single hiriq dot; the second word אֲדֹנִים has hiriq. Order and all other points match both readings.

Printed left-to-right order is בַּאדֹנִי first, then וַאדֹנִי, then לַאדֹנִי next to the semicolon (B's order, not A's); but the last word carries a single dot (hiriq) under the nun, not tsere as B has. A's vowels are right, B's order is right, so neither is fully correct.

Under the initial bet (which carries a dagesh) the print shows a single round dot (hiriq), not a horizontal patah bar; the rest (shewa under lamed, hataf-patah under alef, qamets under dalet, final nun) is identical in both readings.

Both readings match the printed letters; the only difference is the encoding of the elision mark after κατ. The print shows a Greek apostrophe (koronis-shaped, set in the Greek font), so A's U+1FBD is the better representation than B's generic U+2019. Hebrew/accents on this line: none to check.

The holem dot in the Tetragrammaton is printed directly above the vav (which also carries the hiriq beneath it), not above the he; the yod carries a plain sheva. Reading B's point placement matches the print.

The only disagreement is the placement of the holem in the Tetragrammaton: the dot is printed above the vav (יֱהוִֹה, holem on vav as in B), not above the preceding he as A encodes; everything else (hateph segol under yod, hiriq under vav, hateph patah/holem/qamets on אֲדֹנָי, the English references and spacing) matches both readings.

The vowel under the ending placeholder has a visible vertical tick beneath the horizontal bar, i.e. qamets (ָ) as in Reading A, not patach (ַ) as in Reading B. Everything else in the line is identical in both readings and matches the print.

The print has a horizontal carrier stroke under which the qamets and patach sit, before each yod (־ָי and ־ַי); Reading B drops this stroke and leaves the vowels hanging on nothing. No dagesh, shin/sin dot or accent is printed; both are Hebrew, not Arabic/Syriac.

Under the nun the print shows a qamets (bar with a descending stem), not a patach — the sense of the passage ("Others consider ָי i. q. ַי") also requires qamets here. The printed line also has a visible space before the semicolon ("plural ;"), which only Reading B preserves.
An acute accent is clearly printed over the second alpha (Βαάλτις); Reading B omits it. Rest of the line is identical in both readings and matches the print.
